title: Rattling under the car
h1: What's that rattling noise under my car?
metaDesc: Rattling from under the car? Answer a few questions to see if it's a heat shield, exhaust hanger, catalytic converter or suspension part, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: rattling noise under car when idling
rattling noise when driving over bumps
sounds like rocks in a can under my car
intro: Most rattles from under a car come from the exhaust system: a loose heat shield, a broken hanger, or loose material inside the catalytic converter. Others come from the suspension or brakes. When it rattles, and what you find with a quick tap test, usually narrows it down. Answer the questions below to find the most likely cause and how soon to act.
safety: If you smell exhaust inside the car, get to fresh air and don't drive it until it's checked. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car.
If something is dragging on the road or hanging down, pull over as soon as it's safe.
Let the car cool for at least an hour before touching anything under it. Exhaust parts get hot enough to burn you.

q_danger.q: Along with the rattle, do you notice any of these?

opts.a: Exhaust smell inside the car, or someone feels dizzy or gets a headache
Something is scraping on the road or hanging down under the car
The check engine light is flashing, or the engine has lost a lot of power
None of these, just the rattle
At a certain engine speed, even when parked (a tinny, buzzing metal rattle)
Mostly at startup or idle, and it fades or changes as the engine warms
Only over bumps or rough roads
Only when braking, or it stops when I press the brake

q_tap.q: With the engine OFF and the exhaust completely cool, tap along the exhaust pipe and its thin metal covers with your hand or a rubber mallet. What happens?
q_tap.help: The exhaust runs from the engine to the tailpipe under the car. Heat shields are thin metal covers above or around the pipe and the catalytic converter (a wider section near the front). Wait at least an hour after driving, and only reach in from the side unless the car is safely on ramps or stands.

opts.a: A thin metal cover buzzes or rattles when I tap it
It sounds like loose gravel or rocks inside a wider section of the exhaust
The pipe swings or knocks against the car, or a rubber hanger is broken
Nothing rattles, or I can't safely reach under the car

result.title: Exhaust may be leaking into the car. Don't drive it
result.now: Get out and get to fresh air. Don't drive the car again until it's repaired. Have it towed or have a mechanic inspect it where it's parked.
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion, get them into fresh air and call 911 or seek medical care.
If the car is parked in a garage, don't run the engine there to listen for the rattle.
result.why: A rattle can come from a broken or loose exhaust part, and the same damage can let exhaust leak out under the car. Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which has no smell of its own and can cause drowsiness and worse. Any exhaust smell in the cabin is a reason to stop.

causes.name: Cracked or broken exhaust pipe or joint
causes.clues: The exhaust is louder than usual, and the rattle is near the front or middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking exhaust manifold or gasket
causes.clues: A ticking or puffing from the engine and a smell when idling.

causes.name: Rusted-through muffler or pipe
causes.clues: Visible holes or heavy rust, and a deeper exhaust sound.

shop: Exhaust leak inspection on a lift
Check body seals and floor for holes

result.title: A part has come loose and may be dragging
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and look from the side of the car. Don't drive on with something dragging. Call roadside assistance or have it towed.
if: If it's a plastic splash shield or panel and you can safely remove or tie it up, that may be enough until it's fixed properly.
If it's the exhaust, don't touch it until it has cooled for at least an hour.
result.why: A part dragging on the road can catch on something, damage other parts, throw sparks or come off and hit other vehicles. The usual culprits are the exhaust after a hanger breaks, or a plastic underbody panel that has torn loose.

causes.name: Broken exhaust hanger or clamp
causes.clues: A metal scraping sound and a louder exhaust.

causes.name: Loose underbody splash shield or panel
causes.clues: A plastic flapping or scraping sound, often after hitting a curb, snow or debris.

causes.name: Loose heat shield
causes.clues: A thin metal sheet hanging down near the exhaust.

you: From the side of the car, look underneath for anything hanging down.

result.title: The part that cleans the exhaust may be breaking up or blocked (catalytic converter)
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Have it towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual) rather than driving on.
if: If you smell burning, see smoke, or notice a strong rotten egg smell, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the light stops flashing, still get it checked before driving any distance.
If the engine stalls, won't rev, or the exhaust or floor area gets very hot, keep the engine off. A blocked or overheated converter can damage the engine and is a fire risk near dry grass or leaves.
result.why: A flashing check engine light means a serious misfire, which sends unburned fuel into the catalytic converter and can overheat it. The inside of the converter can then crack apart and rattle, and loose pieces can block the exhaust, which causes a big loss of power.

causes.name: Engine misfire overheating the converter
causes.clues: A flashing check engine light, shaking, or a fuel or rotten egg smell.

causes.name: Broken-up converter blocking the exhaust
causes.clues: Power has dropped steadily, and the engine struggles to rev.

causes.name: Collapsed muffler inside
causes.clues: A rattle further back, with power loss.

you: If you have a code reader, read and save the codes.

result.title: A loose suspension link, exhaust hanger or underbody panel is a common cause
result.now: Book an inspection when convenient. Tell the shop the rattle only happens over bumps and rough roads.
if: If the steering feels loose, wanders, or a front wheel clunks hard over bumps, stop driving and have it inspected before driving further.
If it becomes a heavier clunk, get it checked within a few days.
If something starts scraping on the road, pull over and look.
If you smell exhaust inside the car, get to fresh air and have it checked before driving again.
result.why: A rattle that only shows up on rough roads means something is loose enough to move when the car bounces. Common possibilities are a worn sway bar link, a sagging exhaust that taps the body, or a loose plastic panel.

causes.name: Worn sway bar link
causes.clues: A light knock or rattle near a wheel on small bumps.

causes.name: Exhaust hitting the body or a loose hanger
causes.clues: A metallic bang under the middle or back of the car, sometimes when shifting into gear too.

causes.name: Loose underbody panel or splash shield
causes.clues: A plastic rattle, often after hitting debris or deep snow.

you: With the car cool and parked, push gently on the tailpipe and see if the exhaust knocks against anything.
Look from the side for loose plastic panels.

result.title: A brake part may be loose or worn
result.now: Have the brakes inspected in the next day or two, and keep driving to a minimum until then. Leave extra stopping distance.
if: If you hear grinding, the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car pulls when braking, or the brake warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you hear a clunk when you first press or release the brake, stop driving and have it inspected. A loose caliper bolt can't be ruled out from here.
If the rattle started right after brake work, call the shop that did the work and have them check it before driving any distance.
result.why: If the rattle changes or stops when you press the brake, the brakes are a likely source. Pads can rattle when the anti-rattle clips are missing or worn, A loose caliper or bracket bolt is less common but more serious, which is why this needs a look soon.

causes.name: Missing or worn anti-rattle clips or pad hardware
causes.clues: A light rattle over bumps that stops when you touch the brake.

causes.name: Loose caliper or bracket bolt
causes.clues: A clunk when you start braking or switch between forward and reverse.

causes.name: Badly worn brake pads
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding when braking.

you: Note whether the rattle stops when you lightly press the brake pedal.

result.title: A loose heat shield is a likely cause
result.now: Look at where the shield is attached. If a bracket has rusted away, the shield can often be secured with a large stainless hose clamp around the pipe. If you're not comfortable doing it, an exhaust shop can usually secure it.
if: If the shield is badly rusted or hanging down, have it repaired or replaced rather than removing it.
If the rattle continues after securing the shield, have the exhaust checked.
If you smell exhaust inside the car, the exhaust gets louder, or anything is hanging down, stop and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Heat shields are thin metal covers that keep exhaust heat away from the floor, fuel lines and dry grass under the car. Their fasteners rust over time, and the loose shield buzzes at certain engine speeds. It's one of the most common rattles under a car.

causes.name: Rusted heat shield fastener or bracket
causes.clues: A tinny buzz at a certain engine speed, even when parked.

causes.name: Loose exhaust clamp
causes.clues: The rattle is at a pipe joint rather than a thin cover.

causes.name: Catalytic converter internal rattle
causes.clues: Tapping the converter itself makes a gravel-like sound.
causes.against: Less likely if the rattle stops when you hold the shield.

you: With the exhaust cool, press on each shield and see whether the rattle stops.
Look for rusted-out fasteners or brackets.
shop: Exhaust and heat shield inspection on a lift

result.title: Parts inside the exhaust cleaner or muffler may be breaking up (catalytic converter)
result.now: Get the exhaust checked within a few days, and avoid long trips and hard acceleration until then.
if: If the engine loses power, struggles to rev, or the check engine light flashes, stop driving and have it towed.
If the check engine light is on steady, ask the shop to check for a misfire too. Misfires are a common reason converters fail.
If you smell burning or a strong rotten egg smell, or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: A catalytic converter has a honeycomb core inside. Heat, age, a hard impact or an engine problem can crack it, and the pieces rattle like gravel in a can, often worst at startup. Over time the broken pieces can block the exhaust and choke the engine.

causes.name: Broken catalytic converter core
causes.clues: A gravel or rock rattle when you tap the converter, often worse at startup or idle.

causes.name: Broken baffle inside the muffler
causes.clues: The gravel sound is from the muffler near the back.

causes.name: Loose heat shield on the converter
causes.clues: The rattle stops when you press on the outer cover.

you: Note whether the engine has lost any power.
Check whether the check engine light is on.

result.title: A broken rubber hanger may be letting the exhaust swing (exhaust hanger or mount)
result.now: Book an exhaust repair within the next week or two. Hangers are usually a simple repair, and catching it early protects the rest of the exhaust.
if: If the exhaust starts hanging low or dragging, pull over and have it towed.
If you smell fumes inside the car, get to fresh air and don't drive it until it's checked.
If the exhaust gets louder, get it checked right away.
result.why: Rubber hangers hold the exhaust in place while letting it move a little. When one breaks, the pipe swings and knocks against the car, especially when starting off or going over bumps. The extra movement can also crack pipes and joints.

causes.name: Broken or stretched rubber hanger
causes.clues: The pipe swings freely, or a hanger is torn or missing.

causes.name: Rusted-off hanger bracket
causes.clues: The rubber is fine, but the metal rod or bracket has broken.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: The exhaust knocks mostly when shifting into gear or taking off.

you: With the exhaust cool, push the tailpipe side to side and listen for knocking.
Look along the pipe for broken rubber hangers.

result.title: A shop should put it on a lift to find the rattle
result.now: Book an inspection when convenient. Tell the shop when the rattle happens: at a certain engine speed, at startup, over bumps or when braking.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, get to fresh air and have it checked before driving again.
If the steering feels loose, the brake pedal feels different, or something is hanging down, stop driving and have it checked first.
If the rattle becomes a clunk, a grind or a scrape, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Under-car rattles are much easier to find with the car lifted, the engine running, and a technician listening and tapping parts. Many turn out to be minor, like a heat shield, but it's worth ruling out exhaust leaks and loose brake or suspension parts.

causes.name: Loose heat shield
causes.clues: A tinny buzz at certain engine speeds.

causes.name: Exhaust hanger or clamp
causes.clues: A knock when starting off or over bumps.

causes.name: Suspension or brake hardware
causes.clues: The rattle happens over bumps or when braking.

you: Record a short video with sound of the rattle, and note the engine speed or road conditions when it happens.
